items.text: Add a part only when a measured problem asks for it. Name the new problem that it brings.
Put slow work on a queue, and answer the user at once.
Exactly once is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent receivers. Apply it on every hop.
Make the idempotency key from the business intent, not from the attempt.
Give urgent and bulk messages separate queues and workers, so a login code never waits.
When reads far outnumber writes, design the read path first, with a cache in front.
Compute the answers of a read-heavy path in advance, such as a top 5 list at each trie node.
Make the store and the device cursors the truth. A push to a device is only the fast path.
Keep the raw events as the system of record. Counts are derived, and you can compute them again.
Write the bytes first, then the metadata. Bytes with no name are harmless. A name with no bytes is not.
Read, then write, on a shared counter is a race. Use an atomic increment or a script, not a lock.
Consistent hashing balances keys, not requests. A hot key needs a cache, copies, or a split.
A clock that goes back can repeat IDs. Wait for a small step. Refuse and alert for a large one.
Last write wins silently drops data. Detect the conflict, and keep both versions, for example as a conflicted copy.
Offset pagination shows posts again when new posts arrive. Use a cursor with a time-sortable ID.
A plain BFS crawl floods one host. Use one queue for each host, with a delay between downloads.
A PSP timeout is an unknown state, not a failure. Retry with the same idempotency key.
Never use floating-point numbers for money. Store integers in the smallest unit, with a currency code.
A label with unbounded values, such as a user ID, makes millions of series. Reject such labels.
With ACK all, an ISR of only the leader protects nothing. Set a minimum ISR, such as 2 of 3.
